title: Visa Cuts 2,600 Jobs as AI Reshapes Payments Industry
excerpt: The payments giant is slashing 7% of its workforce, primarily in technology and product teams, as artificial intelligence accelerates changes across the financial services sector. The cuts come as Indian employees account for a significant share of Visa's tech workforce.
body:
• Visa announced plans to cut 2,600 jobs, or 7% of its workforce, with technology and product teams bearing the brunt of the reductions
  • CEO Ryan McInerney cited AI-driven efficiency gains and a "once-in-a-lifetime inflection point in payments" as drivers of the restructuring
  • The layoffs follow similar moves by Mastercard, Block, and other fintech firms, reflecting an industry-wide shift toward leaner, AI-augmented operations
  • Indian tech professionals on H-1B visas face particular vulnerability, with a strict 60-day grace period to find new sponsorship or leave the US

An Industry in Transformation

Visa, the world's largest payments processor, announced on July 28 that it would eliminate approximately 2,600 positions — about 7% of its global workforce — as it moves to restructure operations around artificial intelligence and emerging payment technologies. The cuts will primarily affect technology and product teams, the company confirmed.

In a memo to employees, CEO Ryan McInerney framed the decision as a necessary response to rapid changes in the payments landscape. "I have deep conviction that we are doing what is right for Visa, our clients and our partners as we continue to focus on driving efficiency across the company in order to reinvest in our highest potential opportunities," McInerney wrote.

"Technology trends are creating a once-in-a-lifetime inflection point in payments that is changing how money moves around the world."

— Ryan McInerney, Visa CEO

The announcement came hours before Visa reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations, with revenue climbing 14% to $11.63 billion and adjusted earnings of $3.32 per share beating analyst estimates of $3.23. Consumer and business spending remained resilient, with payments volume and processed transactions both rising 10% year over year.

A Pattern Across the Industry

Visa's workforce reduction follows a wave of similar cuts across the payments and financial technology sectors. Earlier this year, Mastercard announced plans to cut 4% of its global workforce, while fintech firm Block eliminated nearly half of its 8,000 employees. On Friday, digital banking platform Chime announced a 10% workforce reduction affecting about 150 employees, also citing AI-driven efficiencies.

The layoffs underscore how companies are translating artificial intelligence investments into tangible workforce changes. AI has helped automate repetitive tasks and accelerate product development, though Bloomberg News reported that it was not the sole factor behind Visa's decision. The company has also been expanding into new verticals, including stablecoins and agentic commerce — technologies that could fundamentally reshape how payments flow.

According to Visa's 2025 annual report, the company had approximately 34,100 employees in fiscal year 2025, up 8% year over year. Analysts at Evercore ISI characterized the cuts as routine optimization. "We don't view this as a material event, as it is just one of the best-run companies in the world tweaking headcount and costs and reallocating money and resources into areas of higher growth and returns," the firm said in a note.

The Diaspora Impact

For Indian technology professionals, who constitute a substantial portion of Visa's engineering and product workforce in both the United States and India, the layoffs carry an additional dimension of risk. Visa operates significant technology centers in Bengaluru and other Indian cities, and its U.S. operations employ a large number of H-1B visa holders.

Indian H-1B workers who lose their positions face a strict 60-day grace period to secure new employer sponsorship or leave the country — a timeline that has become increasingly difficult to meet as hiring across the tech sector slows. Data compiled by industry trackers shows that more than 114,000 technology jobs have been eliminated across nearly 150 companies in 2026 alone.

The pressure on displaced workers extends far beyond income loss. "Families are now dealing with mortgage payments, apartment leases, children in schools, and uncertain immigration timelines all at once, with only 60 days to resolve it," immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna told VisaVerge. Visa's shares were up roughly 1% in trading following the announcement, with the company's market capitalization standing at about $683 billion.
